learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and it snaps back; squeeze a lump of atta dough and it stays squashed. Same push, very different materials.
points: A rigid body is only an idealisation: every real body deforms (changes shape or size) when forces act on it.
Elasticity: the property of a body to regain its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.
Plasticity: the body does not regain its shape and is permanently deformed.
Elastic examples: steel, rubber (within limits); nearly plastic examples: putty, wet clay, mud, dough.
Engineers must know elastic behaviour to design bridges, buildings, cranes, machines and even artificial body parts.

example.q: A steel spring is stretched slightly and released; a clay ball is pressed and released. Classify each behaviour.
steps: The spring returns to its original length: elastic.
The clay keeps its new dented shape: plastic.
So steel (within limits) is elastic and clay is plastic.

learn.reallife: The pottery artisans of Khurja rely on the plasticity of wet clay to shape cups and vases on the wheel.

learn.hook: A heavy train crossing the Chenab rail bridge sets up stresses inside every steel member. Engineers calculate each one.
points: When a body is deformed, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area = F/A. SI unit N m⁻² = pascal (Pa).
Longitudinal stress: force normal to the cross-section. Tensile stress when stretched, compressive stress when compressed.
Shearing (tangential) stress: force parallel to the surface (e.g. pushing the top of a book sideways).
Hydraulic (volume) stress: equal force per unit area on all sides (e.g. a body deep in water); it equals the pressure.

learn.hook: Hang a 1 kg mass on a 1 m steel wire and it stretches less than a hair's width. Strain measures that tiny change as a fraction.
points: Strain = fractional change in size or shape. Longitudinal strain = ΔL/L; shearing strain = Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ; volume strain = ΔV/V.
Strain is a ratio of like quantities, so it has no units or dimensions.
Hooke's law: for small deformations, stress ∝ strain, i.e. stress = k × strain.
The proportionality constant k is the modulus of elasticity (Young's, shear or bulk modulus, depending on the type of stress).
Hooke's law is an empirical law and holds only within the elastic (proportional) limit.

teach.nudge: Is strain the stretch itself or a ratio? When does Hooke's law hold?

learn.hook: Testing labs pull a steel rod until it snaps, plotting stress against strain. That curve tells engineers everything about the metal.
points: For a metal under tension, the curve starts as a straight line (O to A): Hooke's law holds up to the proportional limit.
Beyond A, up to the yield point (elastic limit) B, the body still returns to its shape but stress is no longer proportional to strain. The stress at B is the yield strength σ_y.
Beyond B is the plastic region: if the load is removed (say at C), the body does not return; the remaining strain is the permanent set.
Stress rises to a maximum, the ultimate tensile strength σ_u (point D); beyond it, the wire thins locally and breaks at the fracture point E, even with less stress.

example.q: On a stress–strain curve, a wire is loaded to point C beyond the yield point and unloaded. What happens?
steps: C lies in the plastic region.
When unloaded, the curve comes down roughly parallel to OA but does not reach O.
The wire keeps a permanent strain called the permanent set.

learn.reallife: Steel plants grade TMT bars for Indian construction by their yield strength, e.g. 'Fe 500' means a yield strength of about 500 MPa.

learn.hook: Copper can be drawn into thin wires; a glass rod just snaps. The stress–strain curve explains why.
points: Ductile materials (copper, aluminium, mild steel) have a large plastic region between the ultimate tensile strength and fracture; they can be drawn into wires.
Brittle materials (glass, cast iron, ceramics) fracture soon after the ultimate tensile strength is reached, with little plastic flow.
Elastomers (rubber, the tissue of the aorta) can be stretched to large strains and still return; their curve has no well-defined linear (Hooke's law) region.
Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber, so for the same stress it strains far less. In the physics sense, steel is MORE elastic than rubber.

example.q: Two wires of the same size, one of steel (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) and one of copper (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), carry equal loads. Which stretches more?
steps: ΔL = FL/(AY), so ΔL ∝ 1/Y for the same F, L, A.

learn.reallife: Electricians in India prefer copper wiring partly because copper is ductile: it bends without cracking during installation.

learn.hook: The steel cables of a lift at a Mumbai high-rise stretch a few millimetres every time people step in. Young's modulus predicts exactly how much.
points: Young's modulus Y = longitudinal stress/longitudinal strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Unit N m⁻² (Pa).
Elongation: ΔL = FL/(AY). Thicker, shorter, stiffer wires stretch less.
Typical values: steel about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; copper about 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa; aluminium about 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa. (B and G values are also tabulated for materials.)
Two wires joined end to end carrying a load: both have the same tension F. Stress in each = F/A for that wire; elongations add up.

example.q: A 2 m steel wire (A = 10⁻⁶ m², Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) holds a 100 N load. Find the elongation.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' overhead wire for electric locomotives is kept under carefully calculated tension, using Young's modulus to control sag and stretch.

learn.hook: At the deepest point of the Indian Ocean, water is under over 700 atmospheres of pressure, yet its volume shrinks by only about 3%.
points: Shear (rigidity) modulus G = shearing stress/shearing strain = (F/A)/(Δx/L) = FL/(AΔx). For most materials G ≈ Y/3.
Shear displacement of a slab: Δx = FL/(AG).
Bulk modulus B = −p/(ΔV/V) (the minus sign makes B positive, since volume decreases when pressure increases). Compressibility k = 1/B.
Solids have the largest B, liquids smaller, gases the smallest: gases are the most compressible.
Water has B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; glass about 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

example.q: Water (B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) is subjected to an extra pressure of 2.2 × 10⁷ Pa. Find the fractional decrease in volume.

learn.reallife: Submarines of the Indian Navy are built to withstand enormous hydraulic stress; their hulls use materials with high bulk modulus.

learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and watch it get thinner. That sideways shrinking, compared with the stretch, is Poisson's ratio.
points: When a wire is stretched, it also gets thinner. Lateral strain = Δd/d; longitudinal strain = ΔL/L.
Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain (magnitudes). It has no units or dimensions; for steel it is about 0.28–0.30.
Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ F ΔL.
Energy density (per unit volume): u = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y (strain)² = (stress)²/(2Y).

learn.hook: Why are bridge girders shaped like the letter I, and why can't mountains on Earth be much taller than about 10 km? Elasticity answers both.
points: Crane ropes: the rope's area must keep stress below the yield strength, with a safety factor (say 10). Ropes are made of many thin wires twisted together for flexibility and strength.

Beams: sag of a beam (length l, breadth b, depth d) loaded at the middle: δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). Increasing depth d reduces sag greatly (d³), so beams are deep; an I-section saves material and resists buckling.
Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends carry more load than those with rounded ends.
Mountains: the rock at the base would flow under shear stress if a mountain were much taller than about 10 km on Earth.
Typical numericals: elongations with Y, shear displacements with G, volume changes with B, and ratios of elongations for different wires.

example.q: A crane must lift 10⁴ kg. The rope's yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum cross-sectional area, and with a safety factor of 10.
steps: With safety factor 10: A ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻³ m² (radius about 3 cm).

learn.reallife: The I-shaped steel girders used in Delhi Metro's elevated viaducts are chosen to resist bending with minimum steel.

teach.nudge: Which dimension of a beam reduces sag the most? How do engineers make sure a rope won't fail?
